title: Preface
summary: Apple Inc.’s Form 10-K cover page identifies its fiscal year ended September 27, 2025; California incorporation, employer ID, Cupertino headquarters, contact details, and SEC file number; and its Nasdaq-listed common stock and notes due 2025–2042. It records filing and issuer-status checkboxes, including large accelerated filer, timely reporting and data submissions, and auditor attestation of internal controls. It reports no Section 12(g) securities, a nonaffiliate market value of about $3.253 trillion as of March 28, 2025, and 14.776 billion shares outstanding as of October 17, 2025.

title: DOCUMENTS INCORPORATED BY REFERENCE
summary: The excerpt outlines Apple’s 2025 Form 10-K, including its contents by report part and the incorporation of 2026 proxy-statement material into Part III. It explains forward-looking-statement risks, identification, and update obligations, and clarifies fiscal-year and Company terminology. Part I introduces Apple’s business, fiscal calendar, and product lines: iPhone, Mac, iPad, wearables, home devices, and accessories, with their operating systems and principal offerings.

title: Apple Business, Products, and Forward-Looking Statements
summary: The page explains that Apple’s forward-looking statements are uncertain, may differ from actual results, are subject to risk factors, and generally need not be updated; it also defines fiscal-year references and “Company”/“Apple.” Apple designs, manufactures, and sells smartphones, computers, tablets, wearables, accessories, and services, with a 52- or 53-week fiscal year ending in September. Product lines include iPhone, Mac, iPad, wearables, headphones, spatial computing, home devices, and branded and third-party accessories.

title: Services, Geographic Segments, and Distribution
key_items: Advertising; AppleCare; Cloud Services; Digital Content; Payment Services
summary: The page outlines the company’s advertising, AppleCare support and repair coverage, cloud storage and syncing, digital content platforms and subscriptions, and payment services. It describes its five geographic reporting segments and how they are managed. It also identifies customer markets and direct and indirect product and service distribution channels, noting that in 2025 these generated 40% and 60% of net sales, respectively.

title: Competition
summary: Apple faces intense, price-driven competition, rapid innovation and product cycles, imitation and IP infringement, and competitors with broad offerings, large customer bases, and low-cost structures; success depends on timely innovation and factors including price, quality, security, design, ecosystem, distribution, support, reputation, and IP protection. Component supply risks include single sources, shortages, price volatility, trade restrictions, custom-part capacity constraints, and supplier or contract disruptions. Apple invests in R&D, licensing, and acquisitions to sustain offerings. It holds and continually pursues global patents, designs, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets, and other rights, while relying chiefly on its employees’ capabilities; no single right protects its products, and protection durations are considered adequate.

title: Competition, Component Supply, and R&D
summary: The Company’s success depends on timely innovation, integrated product development, and competing on price, features, quality, design, ecosystem, distribution, support, reputation, and intellectual property. It faces intense competition, imitation, price pressure, minority market shares, and slow or contracting markets. Component supply risks include limited sources, shortages, price fluctuations, trade restrictions, custom-component and capacity constraints, and supplier or contract uncertainty. R&D, licensing, and acquisitions support continued technological advances and expanded offerings.

title: Intellectual Property
summary: The Company describes its global portfolio of patents, designs, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets and other IP, ongoing applications, reliance on employee innovation, and need for third-party licenses that may not remain available on reasonable terms. Sales fluctuate with holiday seasonality, product launches and channel inventory. Its human-capital approach covers recruiting and inclusion, roughly 166,000 employees, compensation and benefits, development, communication and workplace safety. SEC filings are freely available online; corporate and investor websites provide company and financial information, which is not incorporated into the filing.

title: Business Factors, Workforce, and Investor Information
summary: The Company may need third-party intellectual-property licenses, whose future availability and terms are uncertain. Seasonality, holiday demand, product launches, channel inventory changes, and launch anticipation affect sales and expenses. Human-capital practices cover talent, inclusion, compensation, benefits, development, communication, employee feedback, and workplace safety; the Company had about 166,000 full-time-equivalent employees on September 27, 2025. SEC filings and investor information are available through the Company’s websites, whose content is not incorporated into the filing.

title: Item 1A. Risk Factors
summary: This section outlines potential risks that could materially harm the Company’s business, reputation, operating results, financial condition, or stock price. The Company may not accurately predict, control, or mitigate them; the listed risks reflect its current beliefs, are not claims about past events, and are not exhaustive. Read them alongside the specified Management’s Discussion and Analysis and consolidated financial statements and notes.

title: Macroeconomic and Industry Risks
key_items: The Company’s operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions and adverse economic conditions can materially adversely affect the Company’s business, results of operations, financial condition and stock price.

The Company’s business can be impacted by political events, trade and other international disputes, geopolitical tensions, conflict, terrorism, natural disasters, public health issues, industrial accidents and other business interruptions.
Global markets for the Company’s products and services are highly competitive and subject to rapid technological change, and the Company may be unable to compete effectively in these markets.
summary: The text outlines Apple’s risks from global economic weakness affecting demand, partners, credit, liquidity and stock value; political, trade and geopolitical conflicts, tariffs and retaliatory measures that could raise costs, restrict products or disrupt concentrated supply chains; and disasters, climate-related extreme weather, accidents, cyberattacks, labor issues and pandemics that may interrupt operations, sales and delivery, with recovery costs potentially uninsured. It also describes intense, fast-changing competition, pricing and margin pressure, the need for successful R&D and innovation, IP infringement and regulatory limits on IP, competitors’ scale and resources, and Apple’s minority market shares, any of which could harm performance and stock value.

title: Business Risks

nodes.title: Product, Outsourcing, and Supply Chain Risks
key_items: To remain competitive and stimulate customer demand, the Company must successfully manage frequent introductions and transitions of products and services.
The Company depends on component and product manufacturing and logistical services provided by outsourcing partners, many of which are located outside of the U.S.
Future operating results depend upon the Company’s ability to obtain components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from managing frequent product and service launches, transitions, demand, quality, technology, production, and inventory; failure could harm business and financial results. It explains reliance on overseas outsourcing partners and single-source manufacturers for components, assembly, and logistics, which reduces control and creates quality, cost, compliance, and operational risks; changing supply chains takes time and resources. It also covers component shortages, price fluctuations, custom and single-source parts, supplier capacity or failure, and challenges securing sufficient components on reasonable terms.

nodes.title: Product, Asset, and Intellectual Property Risks
key_items: The Company’s products and services may be affected from time to time by design and manufacturing defects that could materially adversely affect the Company’s business and result in harm to the Company’s reputation.
The Company is exposed to the risk of write-downs on the value of its inventory and other assets, in addition to purchase commitment cancellation risk.
The Company relies on access to third-party intellectual property, which may not be available to the Company on commercially reasonable terms, or at all.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from defects in products, software, services, components, and emerging technologies, including safety and security issues, outages, liability, recalls, costs, reputational damage, and lost sales. It covers inventory and asset write-downs or impairments, plus excess orders and cancellation fees caused by volatile markets and inaccurate forecasts. It also explains reliance on third-party intellectual property, potential infringement claims, difficulty obtaining licenses, and resulting product changes, sales restrictions, costs, and financial or reputational harm.

nodes.title: Key Business Risks: Developers, Content, and Talent
key_items: The Company’s future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers.

Failure to obtain or create digital content that appeals to the Company’s customers, or to make such content available on commercially reasonable terms, could have a material adverse impact on the Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition.

The Company’s success depends largely on the talents and efforts of its team members, the continued service and availability of highly skilled employees, including key personnel, and the Company’s ability to nurture its distinctive and inclusive culture.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from reduced third-party developer support, which could limit application availability and quality and weaken product demand; inability to license or produce appealing digital content on reasonable terms; and challenges recruiting and retaining skilled employees amid competition, changing workforce dynamics, and regulation. Failure to sustain the Company’s distinctive, inclusive culture could also harm talent retention and business performance.

nodes.title: Reseller and Technology Risks
key_items: The Company depends on the performance of carriers and other resellers.
The Company’s business and reputation are impacted by information technology system failures and network disruptions.
nodes.summary: The Company relies on carriers and resellers, which also sell competitors’ products and may change or end device financing and subsidies. Investments in reseller sales, staffing, displays, and marketing may not generate returns; changing consumer demand, reseller financial weakness, distribution changes, or reduced orders and marketing could harm business and financial performance. The Company and its supply chain also face IT failures and network disruptions from varied hazards and cyber incidents. Continuity measures and recovery plans may prove inadequate, disrupting online services, customer transactions, manufacturing, or shipping and damaging reputation and financial results.

nodes.title: Losses or unauthorized access to or releases of confidential information, including personal information, could subject the Company to significant reputational, financial, legal and operational consequences.
nodes.summary: The Company’s use, storage, and sharing of sensitive customer and employee data expose it to breaches, unauthorized disclosure, and malicious attacks despite substantial security measures, including encryption and controls for third parties. Attacks may disrupt operations, harm reputation, finances and stock price, damage relationships, reduce customer access or orders, and lead to litigation, investigations, fines or judgments. Threats are frequent, growing in sophistication, heightened by geopolitical conflict, and particularly target the high-profile Company and valuable data. Risks also include ransomware, hacking, employee or system errors, weak password practices, and fraud. Multifactor authentication, monitoring, and account freezes help protect systems but can inconvenience customers; insurance may not cover all losses or claims.

nodes.title: Investment in new business strategies, commercial relationships and acquisitions could disrupt the Company’s ongoing business, present risks not originally contemplated, and materially adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations and financial condition.
nodes.summary: The Company’s investments in new strategies, commercial relationships, and acquisitions may disrupt ongoing operations and expose it to management distraction, unexpected liabilities and expenses, challenges in new markets, poor returns, asset impairments, and write-offs. Transactions may face delayed or denied regulatory approvals, counterparty failures, or onerous conditions that hinder completion or benefits. These inherently risky ventures may fail, materially harming the Company’s business, reputation, results, financial condition, and stock price.

summary: The section covers risks from product launches, outsourcing, supply-chain dependence, shortages, quality defects, technology, inventory and intellectual property; reliance on developers, content providers, resellers, and skilled employees, including the need to sustain company culture; and IT disruptions, cybersecurity attacks, and exposure of confidential or personal data. It also addresses investments, commercial relationships, and acquisitions that may disrupt operations, fail to deliver expected benefits, or cause financial, legal, operational, and reputational harm.

title: Legal and Regulatory Compliance Risks

nodes.title: The Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition could be adversely impacted by unfavorable results of legal proceedings or government investigations.
nodes.summary: The Company faces increasing litigation, investigations, indemnity claims and patent disputes, including those involving emerging AI technologies. Outcomes are uncertain; defense, settlements, damages, injunctions, business restrictions and inadequate insurance could harm operations, finances, reputation and stock price. Complex, changing global laws across many sectors create costly compliance demands, uncertainty and risks of penalties, product or trade restrictions, and required business or supply-chain changes, especially in specialized markets and AI. Conflicting stakeholder expectations and environmental or social commitments also create investment, delivery, legal, reputational and financial risks if goals are unmet or actions are perceived as misaligned.

nodes.title: Legal, Regulatory and Stakeholder Risks
key_items: The Company is subject to complex and changing laws and regulations worldwide, which exposes the Company to potential liabilities, increased costs and other adverse effects on the Company’s business.
Varied stakeholder expectations about social and other issues expose the Company to potential liabilities, increased costs, reputational harm, and other adverse effects on the Company’s business.
nodes.summary: Litigation and investigations have uncertain outcomes that may cause substantial financial, operational, reputational and stock-price harm; insurance may not cover all claims. Complex, changing global laws and enforcement priorities impose costly compliance, constrain products and operations, and create uncertainty, with heightened risks in specialized sectors and emerging technologies. Regulatory changes may arrive without notice, and violations can lead to import restrictions or product bans. Differing stakeholder expectations and environmental or social commitments carry costs and uncertainty; unmet, perceived unmet, or conflicting expectations may trigger backlash and legal proceedings.

nodes.title: The technology industry, including, in some instances, the Company, is subject to intense media, political and regulatory scrutiny, which exposes the Company to increasing regulation, government investigations, legal actions and penalties.
nodes.summary: The technology sector, including Apple, faces heightened media, political and regulatory scrutiny, investigations, litigation and penalties. Apple has changed and expects to further change its business in response to legal, competitive and market pressures; U.S. App Store changes include developer communications about alternative purchases and a court order barring fees on certain purchases. Globally, competition laws—especially the EU Digital Markets Act—have prompted changes to Apple’s platforms, distribution, payments, fees and developer tools; its compliance plan is contested, and risks, fines and adverse business effects remain. Apple faces antitrust cases and investigations worldwide, while proceedings against business partners, notably Google’s search arrangements and antitrust remedies subject to further proceedings and appeal, could reduce licensing revenue. Outcomes and compliance changes may harm privacy and security perceptions, user experience, reputation, competitiveness, demand, sales, margins, financial results and stock price.

nodes.title: The Company’s business is subject to a variety of U.S. and international laws, rules, policies and other obligations regarding the collection, use, protection and transfer of personal data.
nodes.summary: The Company faces expanding and inconsistent U.S. and international privacy and data-protection laws governing personal data, including cross-border transfers. Compliance can require substantial costs and business changes; violations or perceived inconsistencies with public privacy statements may lead to penalties, investigations, audits, legal liability and reputational harm, with new technologies such as AI increasing disclosure risks. Additional rules cover minors and sensitive health, biometric, financial and payment-card data, including security, breach-notification and audit obligations. Changing online-safety laws, including age verification and protections for minors, may require major operational and product changes, raise costs and risks, disrupt operations, and adversely affect business, financial results and stock price.

summary: The Company faces uncertain litigation, investigations, patent and indemnity claims, and heightened scrutiny of the technology sector, potentially causing penalties, restrictions, costly business changes, reputational damage, and financial or stock-price harm; insurance may be inadequate. Complex, changing global laws—including competition rules and privacy, data-transfer, online-safety, and protections for minors and sensitive data—raise compliance costs and risks, especially for emerging technologies such as AI. U.S. and international antitrust actions and regulatory changes may affect platforms, distribution, payments, fees, partners, privacy, security, user experience, demand, and revenue. Conflicting stakeholder expectations and environmental or social commitments also create costs and legal, operational, reputational, and financial risks.

title: Financial Risks
key_items: The Company’s net sales and gross margins are subject to volatility and downward pressure due to a variety of factors.
The Company’s financial performance is subject to risks associated with changes in the value of the U.S. dollar relative to local currencies.
The Company is exposed to credit risk and fluctuations in the values of its investment portfolio.

The Company is exposed to credit risk on its trade accounts receivable, vendor non-trade receivables and prepayments related to long-term supply agreements, and this risk is heightened during periods when economic conditions worsen.
The Company is subject to changes in tax rates, the adoption of new U.S. or international tax legislation and exposure to additional tax liabilities.
summary: The text outlines financial risks including volatility in sales and margins from pricing pressure, competition, demand, product cycles, supply and costs, quality, product/geographic/channel mix, currencies, inflation, tariffs, and new offerings; dependence on a major product category; foreign-exchange effects on sales, costs, pricing, margins, and hedging effectiveness; investment portfolio value and liquidity risks; customer, reseller, vendor-receivable, and supply-prepayment credit exposure; and tax-rate, tax-law, interpretation, and audit uncertainties that could increase liabilities. These risks may materially harm results, financial condition, or stock price.

title: Stock Risks, Cybersecurity and Properties
key_items: The price of the Company’s stock is subject to volatility.
Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments; Item 1C. Cybersecurity; Item 2. Properties
summary: The page describes stock-price volatility and how unmet growth, profitability, dividend, repurchase, or market expectations could harm investor confidence and employee retention; reports no unresolved staff comments; outlines cybersecurity leadership, security-team duties, supplier and incident-risk processes, enterprise risk management, and Audit Committee and Board oversight; and notes the company’s Cupertino headquarters and worldwide facilities, which it considers suitable and in good condition.

title: Item 3. Legal Proceedings
key_items: Digital Markets Act Investigations; Department of Justice Lawsuit; Epic Games; Other Legal Proceedings
summary: The Company faces EU DMA investigations: a €500 million fine and cease-and-desist order over App Store steering rules, which it appealed, and a separate investigation with preliminary findings that could lead to further orders and fines. It says it complies and is revising its plan. The DOJ and states sued over alleged smartphone monopolization; related U.S. antitrust suits seek damages and other relief, and the Company plans to defend. In Epic Games litigation, a court found an injunction violation, imposed restrictions on fees and steering, denied the Company’s request to modify the injunction, and referred the matter for possible criminal contempt. The Company appealed; expedited arguments were heard in October 2025. Other ordinary-course matters remain unresolved; some were settled without material impact, though adverse outcomes could materially affect results.

title: Item 4. Mine Safety Disclosures
summary: Item 4 reports that mine safety disclosures are not applicable. Item 5 states Apple common stock trades on Nasdaq under AAPL and had 22,429 shareholders of record as of October 17, 2025. For the quarter ended September 27, 2025, Apple repurchased 89.498 million shares in open-market and privately negotiated transactions at monthly average prices of $210.43, $224.25, and $238.56. The filing describes the 2024 $110 billion repurchase program, whose remaining $19.8 billion was used in the fourth quarter, and the 2025 $100 billion program, of which $221 million had been used by quarter-end; neither requires minimum purchases, and purchases may use Rule 10b5-1 plans.

title: Stock Listing, Shareholders, and Repurchases
key_items: Item 5. Market for Registrant’s Common Equity, Related Stockholder Matters and Issuer Purchases of Equity Securities
Purchases of Equity Securities by the Issuer and Affiliated Purchasers
summary: Apple’s common stock trades on Nasdaq under AAPL, and it had 22,429 shareholders of record as of October 17, 2025. During the quarter ended September 27, 2025, it repurchased 89.498 million shares in open-market and privately negotiated transactions at average prices of $210.43, $224.25, and $238.56 across the three monthly periods. Apple completed the remaining $19.8 billion of its May 2024 $110 billion program during the fourth quarter of 2025; $221 million of its May 2025 $100 billion program had been used by September 27. Repurchases have no minimum requirement and may occur through open-market or private transactions, including Rule 10b5-1 plans.

title: Stock Performance and Reserved Item 6
summary: Compares five-year dividend-reinvested cumulative shareholder returns for Apple, the S&P 500, and the Dow Jones U.S. Technology Total Stock Market Index, assuming $100 invested at the September 25, 2020 market close. Reported values run from September 2020 through September 2025; past performance does not predict future results. Item 6 is reserved.

title: 2025 Management Discussion, Announcements, and Conditions
key_items: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
summary: The MD&A directs readers to the financial statements and notes and explains that it covers 2025 and 2024 comparisons, with earlier analysis referenced in the prior annual report. It lists major fiscal 2025 product, service, and software announcements by quarter. It explains the company’s 52- or 53-week fiscal-year schedule, noting 2025 and 2024 had 52 weeks and 2023 had 53. Inflation, interest rates, and currency fluctuations have affected and may materially affect results and financial condition.

title: Tariffs and Other Measures
summary: Since Q2 2025, the U.S. has announced tariffs on imports from multiple countries, prompting reciprocal tariffs and other retaliation; further changes, including sector-specific measures, remain possible. A Section 232 investigation covers semiconductors, manufacturing equipment, and related products. Tariffs may harm the Company’s supply chain, access to raw materials and components, pricing, margins, operations, and financial condition. Their uncertain impact depends on future measures, retaliation, scale, and duration. International disputes may also weaken the broader economy, consumer spending, and sentiment toward the Company’s products and services.

title: Segment Operating Performance
key_items: iPhone; Mac; iPad; Wearables, Home and Accessories
Products Gross Margin; Services Gross Margin
summary: The text reports Apple’s 2025–2023 sales by region and product/service category, with year-over-year changes and explanations. 2025 regional sales rose overall, with growth in the Americas, Europe, Japan, and Rest of Asia Pacific, offset by Greater China’s decline; product sales increased overall, led by iPhone, Mac, iPad, and Services, while Wearables, Home and Accessories fell. It presents product and Services gross margins and percentages, explains 2025 changes, and cautions that future margins may be volatile and face downward pressure. It also reports operating expenses and their percentages of sales, noting R&D growth from headcount and infrastructure costs and SG&A growth from headcount and variable selling expenses.

title: Operating Expenses
summary: The text reports Apple’s 2025, 2024 and 2023 product and services gross margins and percentages. In 2025, product margin rose on favorable costs and product mix, partly offset by tariffs, while its percentage fell due to mix and tariffs; services margin and percentage increased, driven by sales growth and service mix, partly offset by costs. The company warns gross margins may remain volatile and face downward pressure. Operating expenses increased in 2025, with R&D growth driven by headcount and infrastructure costs and selling, general and administrative growth by headcount and variable selling expenses. It also reports income tax provisions and rates: 2025’s effective rate was below the statutory rate due to foreign earnings, R&D credits and share-based compensation benefits, partly offset by valuation allowance and state taxes. Its rate fell from 2024 largely due to a $10.7 billion year-over-year decrease in tax provision related to the State Aid Decision and changes in unrecognized tax benefits, partly offset by valuation allowance and higher foreign tax rates.

title: Liquidity and Capital Resources
key_items: Debt; Leases; Manufacturing Purchase Obligations; Other Purchase Obligations; Deemed Repatriation Tax Payable
summary: The Company expects $132.4 billion in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities, operating cash flow, and debt-market access to cover cash needs and capital returns for the next 12 months and beyond. At September 27, 2025, obligations included $91.3 billion of fixed-rate debt ($12.4 billion due within a year) and $37.0 billion of interest ($2.6 billion due within a year); $8.0 billion of commercial paper; $16.8 billion in leases ($2.6 billion due within a year); $56.2 billion in manufacturing purchases ($55.4 billion due within a year); $14.8 billion in other purchases ($7.0 billion due within a year); and $8.8 billion of deemed repatriation tax due within a year. The share repurchase program has no minimum purchase requirement. In May 2025, the Company authorized up to $100 billion in repurchases and raised its quarterly dividend to $0.26 per share, with annual increases intended subject to Board approval. In 2025, it repurchased $89.3 billion of shares and paid $15.4 billion in dividends and equivalents.

title: Recent Accounting Pronouncements
key_items: Internal-Use Software; Disaggregation of Income Statement Expenses; Income Taxes
summary: The Company discusses three new FASB standards. ASU 2025-06 modernizes internal-use software accounting, removing development-stage references and requiring capitalization when management commits to a project and completion and intended use are probable; it is effective in Q1 2029, permits early adoption, and the Company is evaluating adoption timing and method. ASU 2024-03, with its effective date clarified by ASU 2025-01, requires specified expense-caption disclosures and selling-expense amounts and definitions; adoption is planned for Q4 2028, prospectively. ASU 2023-09 expands income-tax rate-reconciliation and taxes-paid disclosures, including jurisdictional detail; adoption is planned for Q4 2026, prospectively.

title: Critical Accounting Estimates
summary: Management’s GAAP financial reporting relies on estimates and judgments based on experience and reasonable assumptions. Uncertain tax positions across U.S. and foreign jurisdictions involve complex laws; reserve outcomes may differ and materially affect results. Legal claims are accrued when losses are probable and estimable, with outcomes potentially material. Market risks include interest rates and foreign exchange. Interest-rate increases can reduce investment fair values and raise debt costs; mitigation may include derivatives and portfolio adjustments. A 100-basis-point rise could reduce investment values by $2.416 billion (2025) or $2.755 billion (2024) and increase annual debt interest by $129 million or $139 million. Currency movements, especially a stronger dollar, can hurt sales, margins, and asset values; hedging and pricing adjustments may mitigate exposure. VAR modeling estimated 95%-confidence, one-day derivative losses of $590 million in 2025 and $538 million in 2024; underlying exposures generally offset derivative changes.

title: Market Risks and Legal Contingencies
key_items: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
summary: The Company discusses uncertain ordinary-course legal claims, its loss-recognition criteria, and potential material effects. It describes interest-rate and foreign-exchange risks and mitigation strategies. A 100-basis-point rate increase could reduce investment fair value by $2,416 million in 2025 ($2,755 million in 2024) and raise annual term-debt interest expense by $129 million ($139 million). A Monte Carlo VAR model estimates 95%-confidence, one-day derivative fair-value losses of up to $590 million in 2025 ($538 million in 2024); underlying exposures generally offset derivative changes.

title: Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
summary: Item 8 indexes Apple’s consolidated financial statements: statements of operations, comprehensive income, shareholders’ equity, and cash flows for fiscal years 2025, 2024, and 2023; balance sheets for 2025 and 2024; notes; and independent auditors’ reports, with page references. Financial statement schedules are omitted because they are inapplicable, immaterial, or included in the statements and notes.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF OPERATIONS
summary: Apple Inc.’s consolidated statements of operations compare fiscal years ended September 28, 2024, September 27, 2025, and September 30, 2023. They report product and services net sales, cost of sales, gross margin, research and development and selling, general and administrative expenses, operating income, other income or expense, pretax income, income tax provision, net income, basic and diluted earnings per share, and the corresponding shares used to calculate per-share amounts. Figures are in millions except shares (thousands) and per-share amounts; accompanying financial statement notes are referenced.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF COMPREHENSIVE INCOME
summary: Apple’s consolidated statements of comprehensive income report net income, other comprehensive income or loss, and total comprehensive income for fiscal years ended September 28, 2024, September 27, 2025, and September 30, 2023. Other comprehensive items include foreign currency translation, derivative gains and losses (fair-value changes and realized amounts), and marketable debt securities gains and losses (fair-value changes and realized amounts), all net of tax. The statements refer readers to the accompanying financial statement notes.

title: Apple Consolidated Balance Sheets
summary: Apple Inc.’s consolidated balance sheets as of September 27, 2025 and September 28, 2024 present current and non-current assets, total assets, current and non-current liabilities, commitments and contingencies, and shareholders’ equity, including common stock, accumulated deficit, and accumulated other comprehensive loss. Figures are in millions except share counts (thousands) and par value; accompanying financial statement notes are referenced.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF SHAREHOLDERS’ EQUITY
summary: Apple’s consolidated statements of shareholders’ equity present beginning and ending balances for fiscal years 2023–2025, in millions, covering common stock and additional paid-in capital, accumulated deficit, accumulated other comprehensive loss, and total shareholders’ equity. Changes include stock issuance, share-based compensation, net income, dividends, equity-award share withholding, repurchases, and other comprehensive income or loss. Dividends declared per share or RSU were $0.94, $0.98, and $1.02, respectively; accompanying financial statement notes apply.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS (intro)
nodes.summary: The text presents Apple’s consolidated cash flows for fiscal 2023–2025, including operating, investing, and financing activities, changes in cash balances, and income taxes paid. It then outlines accounting policies: consolidated statements use GAAP estimates and may reclassify prior figures; fiscal years end on the last Saturday of September, with 2023 comprising 53 weeks. Apple adopted updated segment-reporting disclosure rules in 2025 retrospectively. Policies cover revenue net of taxes, share-based compensation, cash equivalents, receivables, marketable securities, inventories, and property, plant, and equipment.

nodes.title: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: Apple’s consolidated statements include the company and wholly owned subsidiaries, use GAAP and management estimates, and reclassify prior-period amounts as needed. Fiscal years end on the last Saturday of September; 2025 and 2024 had 52 weeks, while 2023 had 53. Apple adopted ASU 2023-07 retrospectively, requiring disclosures about significant segment expenses, the CODM, and use of segment results. Revenue excludes taxes remitted to authorities; share-based compensation is recognized straight-line for awards expected to vest. Cash equivalents mature within three months; receivables are stated at transaction price; securities use specific identification for cost; inventories use FIFO; and property and equipment are recorded at cost and depreciated straight-line.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments; Income Taxes; Leases
nodes.summary:
Derivative Instruments
The Company presents derivative assets and liabilities at their gross fair values in the Consolidated Balance Sheets.
Income Taxes
The Company records certain deferred tax assets and liabilities in connection with the minimum tax on certain foreign earnings created by the TCJA.
Leases
The Company combines and accounts for lease and nonlease components as a single lease component for leases of corporate and retail facilities.

nodes.title: Note 2 – Revenue
nodes.summary: Revenue is recognized when control transfers: generally upon shipment for products and over time as services are delivered, with payment collected soon afterward. Product sales are reduced for expected returns, price protection, and incentives. Revenue for multiple distinct obligations is allocated using relative standalone selling prices, observed when available or estimated using relevant pricing, market, business, and cost factors. iPhone, Mac, and iPad sales include hardware/software recognized at shipment and bundled services deferred and recognized over their estimated delivery period. Unbilled, undelivered long-term services are not recognized or disclosed. Third-party products are reported gross when Apple obtains control; App Store applications are reported net of retained commissions. Net sales by product and services category are provided for 2023–2025, along with sales previously deferred, segment mix observations, and deferred revenue balances and expected recognition timing.

nodes.title: Note 3 – Earnings Per Share
nodes.summary: Note 3 reports basic and diluted EPS, net income and weighted-average share counts for 2025–2023; about 24 million RSUs were excluded in 2023 as antidilutive. Note 4 details cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities by investment category, fair value hierarchy, valuation inputs and balance-sheet classification for September 2025 and 2024, including prior-year escrow restrictions tied to the State Aid Decision. It also gives maturity distributions for 2025 non-current debt securities and states that marketable debt securities are available-for-sale, classified current or non-current by maturity.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments and Hedging
nodes.summary: The Company uses derivatives selectively to mitigate foreign-exchange and interest-rate risks, though hedges may be incomplete or uneconomic. Derivatives are recorded at fair value; accounting depends on designation: cash-flow hedge gains/losses are deferred in OCI and later reclassified, fair-value hedge effects are recognized with offsetting changes in hedged items, excluded amounts are recognized over the hedge term with fair-value changes in OCI, and undesignated changes enter earnings. Derivative cash flows generally follow the hedged item’s cash-flow classification. Foreign-exchange hedges cover forecast revenue and inventory exposures (typically up to 12 months), foreign-currency debt and securities (up to 17 years for designated debt-related cash flows), and certain remeasurement exposures; interest-rate swaps, options, or other instruments hedge debt and securities. Notional amounts in 2025 versus 2024 were $62.647 billion versus $64.069 billion for designated foreign-exchange contracts, $12.875 billion versus $14.575 billion for designated interest-rate contracts, and $109.079 billion versus $91.493 billion for undesignated foreign-exchange contracts. Debt subject to fair-value hedges was $12.6 billion versus $13.5 billion.

nodes.title: Accounts Receivable
nodes.summary: As of September 27, 2025, one customer represented 12% of trade receivables; third-party cellular carriers represented 34%, down from 38% in 2024. The Company obtains credit support or collateral from some customers. Vendor non-trade receivables arise from components sold to manufacturing vendors; gains reduce product cost of sales when the related products are sold, rather than being recorded as product revenue. Two vendors represented at least 10% each of these receivables in both years: 46% and 23% in 2025, versus 44% and 23% in 2024.

nodes.title: Note 5 – Property, Plant and Equipment
nodes.summary: Note 5 reports property, plant and equipment by asset class for 2025 and 2024, accumulated depreciation, net balances, and depreciation expense for 2023–2025. Note 6 presents comparative balances for other non-current assets and other current liabilities. Note 7 describes the European Commission’s Irish state-aid decision, its appeal and 2024 confirmation, and the resulting $10.2 billion net tax charge. It also details federal, state and foreign current and deferred income-tax provisions, total tax provisions for 2023–2025, and foreign pretax earnings for those years.

nodes.title: Financial Statement Details and European State Aid
nodes.summary: The page presents 2025 and 2024 consolidated balances for other non-current assets and other current liabilities, including deferred tax assets, taxes payable, and accrued distribution and marketing. It recounts the European Commission’s 2016 State Aid Decision concerning Irish tax opinions, the Company and Ireland’s appeals, the 2024 ECJ ruling upholding the decision, and the resulting $10.2 billion net income tax charge, including the escrow payment, U.S. foreign tax credit, and reduction in unrecognized tax benefits.

nodes.title: Provision for Income Taxes and Effective Tax Rate
nodes.summary: Presents Apple’s income tax provision by federal, state, and foreign current and deferred components for 2025, 2024, and 2023, along with foreign pretax earnings of $82.0 billion, $77.3 billion, and $72.9 billion, respectively. It also introduces a reconciliation of each year’s tax provision to the 21% statutory federal rate, covering expected tax, foreign subsidiary earnings, valuation allowance changes, research and development credits, the State Aid Decision, other items, and the effective tax rate.

nodes.title: Deferred Tax Assets and Liabilities
nodes.summary: The text reports deferred tax assets and liabilities, including their components and net balances for 2025 and 2024. At September 27, 2025, net deferred tax assets were $19.98 billion, compared with $19.20 billion in 2024. Major assets include capitalized R&D, tax credit carryforwards, accrued liabilities, deferred revenue, and lease liabilities; liabilities include depreciation, right-of-use assets, and minimum tax on foreign earnings. The company had $4.7 billion of Irish foreign tax credits and $4.0 billion of California R&D credits, both carried forward indefinitely, with valuation allowances against credit carryforwards and some temporary differences.

nodes.title: Uncertain Tax Positions
nodes.summary: Gross unrecognized tax benefits were $23.2 billion at September 27, 2025 ($10.6 billion of which would affect the effective tax rate), versus $22.0 billion at September 28, 2024 ($10.8 billion rate impact). A 2023–2025 reconciliation shows annual changes from prior- and current-year tax positions, settlements, and statute expirations, ending at $23.2 billion, $22.0 billion, and $19.5 billion, respectively. The Company files in U.S. federal, state, and foreign jurisdictions; specified federal and major foreign tax years remain examinable. Benefits could decrease by up to $6 billion within 12 months.

nodes.title: Note 8 – Leases
nodes.summary: Note 8 describes leases for equipment and corporate, data center, manufacturing, and retail facilities, typically with terms up to 10 years and renewal options. It reports fixed and variable lease costs, fixed cash payments, and noncash ROU asset additions for 2023–2025; operating and finance ROU assets and liabilities by balance-sheet line item in 2024 and 2025; 2025 lease-liability maturities and imputed interest; remaining lease terms and discount rates; and $523 million of fixed obligations for leases not yet commenced, expected to begin in 2026–2027. The text then begins Note 9, Debt.

nodes.title: Commercial Paper
nodes.summary: The text describes the Company’s unsecured commercial paper program, its corporate uses, outstanding balances and weighted-average rates for 2025 and 2024, and net proceeds and repayments by maturity for 2025–2023. It summarizes senior unsecured term Notes, including issuances, maturities, principal, effective rates, premiums and issuance costs, hedge adjustments, current and non-current portions, and future principal payments. It also explains interest-rate and cross-currency swaps and reports Notes’ Level 2 fair values for 2025 and 2024, then begins Note 10 on shareholders’ equity.

nodes.title: Share Repurchase Program
nodes.summary: In 2025, Apple repurchased 402 million shares for $89.3 billion; its repurchase programs require no minimum purchases and allow negotiated or open-market transactions, including Rule 10b5-1 plans. The text reports common-stock balances and changes from 2023–2025, including repurchases and net issuances after employee-tax withholdings. It also describes the shareholder-approved 2022 Employee Stock Plan, its eligible awards, typical four-year vesting and one-for-one share settlement of RSUs, dividend equivalent rights, and authorization of about 1.3 billion shares.

nodes.title: Restricted Stock Units
nodes.summary: The text reports Apple’s 2025 RSU activity: 163.326 million opening units, 73.466 million granted, 76.845 million vested, and 8.373 million forfeited, leaving 151.574 million RSUs; corresponding weighted-average grant-date values were $158.73, $226.68, $159.85, $183.03, and $189.75. Grant-date values were $173.78 in 2024 and $150.87 in 2023, based on the stock closing price on grant date. Vesting-date fair values were $17.1 billion, $15.8 billion, and $15.9 billion in 2025, 2024, and 2023; most vested units were net-settled for employee taxes, with $6.1 billion paid to tax authorities in 2025 and $5.6 billion in each prior year. Share-based compensation expense was $12.863 billion, $11.688 billion, and $10.833 billion, with related tax benefits of $3.602 billion, $3.350 billion, and $3.421 billion, respectively. Unrecognized RSU compensation cost was $21.8 billion, expected to be recognized over 2.5 years.

nodes.title: Share-Based Compensation
nodes.summary: The excerpt reports common-stock changes for 2023–2025, then describes Apple’s 2022 employee equity plan, RSU vesting terms and 2025 activity, grant-date and vesting values, tax withholding, share-based compensation expense and tax benefits, and unrecognized RSU compensation. It also lists future unconditional purchase obligations, states management’s assessment of legal contingencies, and explains supply risks from limited sources, shortages, trade restrictions, custom components, supplier constraints, and the geographic concentration of outsourced hardware manufacturing.

nodes.title: Commitments, Contingencies, and Supply Risks
key_items: Concentrations in the Available Sources of Supply of Materials and Product
nodes.summary: The Company reports $13.308 billion in future payments for unconditional purchase obligations, mainly supplier arrangements, licensed intellectual property and content, and distribution rights. It faces ordinary-course legal claims, but management considers material losses beyond recorded accruals not reasonably possible. Supply risks include single-source and custom components, shortages, price fluctuations, trade restrictions, capacity constraints, supplier failures or consolidation, and difficulty renewing agreements or securing timely alternatives. Most hardware is manufactured by outsourcing partners primarily across Asia.

nodes.title: Note 13 – Segment Information and Geographic Data
nodes.summary: Apple manages its business geographically, with its CEO as CODM and five reportable segments: Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, and Rest of Asia Pacific. The CODM uses segment sales and operating income to guide pricing and sales and marketing resource allocation; segment reporting excludes assets. The text provides 2023–2025 segment sales, costs, expenses, and operating income, plus country-level net sales for the U.S., China, and other countries and long-lived assets for 2024–2025. China includes Hong Kong and Taiwan.

summary: Presents Apple’s 2023–2025 cash flows and significant accounting policies, then details revenue, EPS, cash and investments, derivatives and hedging, receivables, property and other balances, income taxes and the European State Aid Decision, deferred taxes and uncertain tax positions, leases, commercial paper and debt, share repurchases and stock compensation, purchase commitments, legal and supply risks, and segment and geographic sales, operating results, and long-lived assets.

title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm

nodes.title: Apple Independent Auditor’s Report
nodes.summary: The auditor gives an unqualified opinion that Apple’s financial statements for fiscal 2025 and the prior year, including three years of operating results and cash flows, fairly present its financial position under U.S. GAAP, and reports an unqualified opinion on internal controls. The report explains management’s and the auditor’s responsibilities, auditor independence, PCAOB audit standards and procedures, and the reasonable-assurance basis for the opinion. It introduces a critical audit matter, noting its criteria and that it does not change or constitute a separate opinion; the provided text ends before describing the matter.

nodes.title: Uncertain Tax Positions
nodes.summary: Apple reported $23.2 billion in gross unrecognized tax benefits as of September 27, 2025, including $10.6 billion that would affect its effective tax rate if recognized; assessing these positions requires complex judgment. EY tested related controls, evaluated management’s analyses, tax-authority communications, technical merits and disclosures, using tax specialists. EY, Apple’s auditor since 2009, also concluded that internal controls over financial reporting were effective in all material respects under COSO criteria. Its report describes management and auditor responsibilities, audit procedures and reasonable-assurance basis, defines these controls, and notes their inherent limitations and risks in projecting effectiveness. EY issued unqualified opinions on the financial statements and internal controls; the reports are dated October 31, 2025.

nodes.title: Apple Internal Control Audit Report
key_items: Opinion on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
Definition and Limitations of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Ernst & Young reports that Apple maintained effective internal control over financial reporting in all material respects as of September 27, 2025, and notes its separate unqualified financial-statement audit opinion. The report explains management’s and the auditor’s responsibilities, PCAOB-compliant audit procedures and reasonable-assurance basis, defines the controls’ purpose and key policies, and describes limitations: controls may not prevent or detect misstatements, and effectiveness may change over time.

nodes.title: Accountants, Disclosure Controls, and Internal Controls
key_items: Item 9. Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants on Accounting and Financial Disclosure
Evaluation of Disclosure Controls and Procedures
Management’s Annual Report on Internal Control over Financial Reporting
Changes in Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: The company reports no disagreements with accountants. Management and the principal executive and financial officers found disclosure controls effective as of September 27, 2025. The page explains internal controls’ purposes and inherent limits, including that they provide reasonable—not absolute—assurance and may weaken as conditions change. Management assessed financial reporting controls under the 2013 COSO framework and found them effective; Ernst & Young issued an audit report. No materially significant control changes occurred in the fourth quarter of 2025.

nodes.title: Other Disclosures and Part III Proxy Statement Items
key_items: Item 9B. Other Information; Insider Trading Arrangements; Item 9C. Disclosure Regarding Foreign Jurisdictions that Prevent Inspections
Item 9C. Disclosure Regarding Foreign Jurisdictions that Prevent Inspections
Item 10. Directors, Executive Officers and Corporate Governance
Item 12. Security Ownership of Certain Beneficial Owners and Management and Related Stockholder Matters
Item 13. Certain Relationships and Related Transactions, and Director Independence
Item 14. Principal Accountant Fees and Services
nodes.summary: Reports the planned January 2026 transition of Apple’s Principal Accounting Officer from Chris Kondo to Ben Borders, who will report to CFO Kevan Parekh; states there are no insider trading arrangements and foreign-inspection disclosure is not applicable. Part III items on directors and governance, executive compensation, ownership and stockholder matters, related transactions and director independence, and accountant fees and services will be addressed in the 2026 Proxy Statement and incorporated by reference.

nodes.title: PART IV
key_items: (3) Exhibits required by Item 601 of Regulation S-K (1)
nodes.summary: Part IV of Apple’s 2025 Form 10-K lists its consolidated financial statements for fiscal years 2023–2025, notes, and Ernst & Young’s audit reports; schedules are omitted because they are inapplicable, immaterial, or covered elsewhere. It inventories exhibits covering corporate governance, debt indentures and notes, compensation and equity plans, insider-trading and recovery policies, subsidiaries, audit consent, powers of attorney, officer certifications, and Inline XBRL files, with incorporation-by-reference details and filing-status markers. Debt-holder instruments may be provided to the SEC upon request. Item 16 states there is no Form 10-K summary.

summary: Ernst & Young gives unqualified opinions that Apple’s fiscal 2025 and comparative financial statements fairly present its financial position under U.S. GAAP and that internal controls were effective. The reports explain audit and management responsibilities, procedures, reasonable assurance, control limitations, and the critical audit matter of uncertain tax positions, including $23.2 billion in unrecognized benefits. The section also covers disclosure controls, no accountant disagreements or material fourth-quarter control changes, an accounting-officer transition, other disclosures, proxy-statement items, and Part IV statements, schedules, exhibits, and the absence of a Form 10-K summary.

title: SIGNATURES
summary: Apple Inc.’s Form 10-K signatures section states that CFO Kevan Parekh signed the report on the company’s behalf on October 31, 2025. It grants Timothy D. Cook and Kevan Parekh joint and several authority, with substitution, to sign and file amendments and related documents, ratifying their actions. The report lists the signatures, titles, and October 31, 2025 signing date for Cook, Parekh, Chris Kondo, and directors Wanda Austin, Alex Gorsky, Andrea Jung, Arthur D. Levinson, Monica Lozano, Ronald D. Sugar, and Susan L. Wagner.

title: DESCRIPTION OF THE REGISTRANT’S SECURITIES REGISTERED PURSUANT TO SECTION 12 OF THE SECURITIES EXCHANGE ACT OF 1934
summary: As of September 27, 2025, Apple had eight securities registered under Section 12 of the Exchange Act: common stock and seven note issues with stated coupon rates and maturities from 2025 to 2042. All are listed on The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC.

title: DESCRIPTION OF COMMON STOCK
key_items: Dividends; Right to Receive Liquidation Distributions; No Preemptive or Similar Rights
Anti-Takeover Provisions of the Articles, Bylaws and California Law; Listing
Anti-Takeover Provisions of the Articles, Bylaws and California Law
summary: The text outlines Apple common stock rights under its Articles, Bylaws, and California law: 50.4 billion shares are authorized, and outstanding shares are fully paid and nonassessable. Each share has one noncumulative vote; it describes approval thresholds, director elections and removal, vacancy filling, amendments, and meeting adjournments. Shareholders may receive board-declared dividends and pro rata liquidation distributions, but have no preemptive, conversion, redemption, or sinking-fund rights. Anti-takeover provisions address director vacancies, advance notice for proposals and nominations, 3% shareholder proxy access, special-meeting calls, and California’s fairness-opinion requirement for interested-party reorganizations. Shares trade on Nasdaq as AAPL.

title: DESCRIPTION OF DEBT SECURITIES

nodes.title: The Notes
key_items: The 2025 Notes; The 2026 Notes; The 2027 Notes; The 1.375% 2029 Notes; The 3.050% 2029 Notes
nodes.summary: The text summarizes Apple’s notes, qualified by its 2013 and 2018 indentures, governed by New York law. The indentures allow unlimited debt issuance and, without existing holders’ consent, additional similar securities that may join a series, subject to ISIN conditions. It lists each note’s issue amount and date, maturity, interest rate and payment schedule, and amount outstanding as of October 17, 2025: €1 billion 2025 notes at 0%; €1.4 billion 2026 at 1.625%; €1 billion 2027 at 2%; €1.25 billion 1.375% 2029; £750 million 3.05% 2029; €1 billion 2031 at 0.5%; and £500 million 2042 at 3.6%.

nodes.title: Ranking
nodes.summary: The Notes rank equally with the issuer’s other senior unsecured, unsubordinated debt, but are structurally subordinated to subsidiary debt and preferred stock and effectively subordinated to secured debt up to the value of collateral. Subsidiary creditors generally have priority over the issuer’s creditors, including Noteholders, regarding subsidiary assets and earnings. The Indentures do not limit the issuer or its subsidiaries from incurring additional debt.

nodes.title: Payment on the Notes
nodes.summary: The 2025, 2026, 2027, 1.375% 2029 and 2031 Notes are payable in euros, but payments switch to U.S. dollars if euros become unavailable or cease qualifying for use, and resume in euros when conditions allow. Conversion uses the Federal Reserve rate or, if none is mandated, the latest Wall Street Journal rate available two Business Days before payment; dollar payments are not defaults. Their Business Day definition excludes weekends, New York or London bank-closing days, and days TARGET2 is closed. The 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes are payable in pounds sterling, or euros if the UK adopts the euro, with the same dollar-payment fallback, conversion method and non-default protection. Their Business Day definition excludes days banks in New York, London or the payment location are closed.

nodes.title: Payment of Additional Amounts
nodes.summary: The Notes generally require principal and interest payments free of U.S. tax withholding unless legally required. For non-U.S. holders, the Company must pay Additional Amounts to preserve the stated net payment, subject to exceptions for holder or beneficial-owner U.S. connections or status; intermediary ownership structures; failure to provide required tax forms or information; non-withholding taxes; late changes in law; specified property, estate, transfer and similar taxes; withholding avoidable through another paying agent; late presentation for payment; and FATCA taxes, including combinations of these exceptions. The Notes remain subject to applicable tax laws, and the Company has no other tax-payment obligation. The text defines the United States and United States person for these provisions and tax-redemption terms.

nodes.title: Redemption for Tax Reasons
nodes.summary: The issuer may redeem an affected Notes series in whole, but not in part, at 100% of principal plus accrued unpaid interest if a post-prospectus U.S. legal or interpretive change causes, or independent counsel confirms will cause, additional tax payments. Notice periods are 30–60 days for the 2026, 2027, 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes; 15–60 days for the 1.375% 2029 Notes; and 10–60 days for the 2025 and 2031 Notes. For the latter two series, interest is calculated excluding the redemption date.

nodes.title: Optional Redemption
nodes.summary: The text sets out optional redemption terms. The 2026, 2027, 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes may be redeemed at any time at the greater of par or the present value of remaining payments, discounted at the applicable government bond rate plus series-specific spreads. The 2025, 1.375% 2029 and 2031 Notes have similar make-whole redemption before their specified Par Call Dates, using payments through the Par Call Date; on or after those dates, they may be redeemed at par. Accrued interest is paid to (but excluding) redemption, while interest already due is paid to record-date holders. The text defines Par Call Dates, the relevant German or UK Comparable Government Bonds, and the bond-rate calculation method.

nodes.title: Covenants
key_items: Consolidation, Merger and Sale of Assets
nodes.summary: The Indentures contain limited covenants and do not restrict incurring debt or leases, issuing debt secured by liens, or paying dividends, making distributions, or repurchasing or redeeming stock. They permit mergers, consolidations, and transfers of substantially all assets if the successor is appropriately U.S.-organized, assumes the obligations and conversion rights, no default exists afterward, and—under the 2013 Indenture—required certificates and a legal opinion are provided. The successor replaces the issuer and assumes its rights and powers; the issuer is released from its obligations. “Person” is broadly defined to include individuals, entities, governments, and their agencies or subdivisions.

nodes.title: Events of Default
nodes.summary: The indentures define defaults for a series as unpaid interest after 30 days; unpaid principal or premium when due; uncured covenant breaches after 90 days’ notice (with holder thresholds of 25% under the 2013 indenture and 33% under the 2018); specified voluntary or court-ordered insolvency events; and any additional series-specific defaults. The text defines Bankruptcy Law and Custodian, explains acceleration and automatic bankruptcy acceleration, majority-holder rescission, series-specific defaults, and the company’s annual compliance statement. It sets conditions and thresholds for holders to bring proceedings, describes majority-holder control over remedies and waivers and the trustee’s duties and indemnity protections, and preserves each holder’s unconditional right to payment and suit to enforce it.

nodes.title: Modification and Waivers
nodes.summary: The text explains Indenture and Note amendments: changes generally require majority approval, while specified fundamental payment, redemption, currency, enforcement, voting, waiver, and conversion rights require each affected holder’s consent. It lists changes the issuer and trustee may make without holder consent, including adding protections, defaults, guarantees, security, trustees or securities, addressing succession, issuance, form, and administrative or legal matters, subject to stated safeguards. It also describes majority-holder waivers of certain covenants and past defaults, excluding payment defaults and provisions requiring unanimous consent; a waiver cures only the specific default and does not affect later defaults.

nodes.title: Discharge, Defeasance and Covenant Defeasance
nodes.summary: The text describes three options for Notes: discharge near-maturity or redemption obligations by depositing sufficient U.S. dollars with the trustee, which may be invested in short-term Treasury securities; legal defeasance, ending most obligations while retaining specified administrative and payment duties; and covenant defeasance, releasing restrictive-covenant obligations and certain default provisions. Defeasance requires an irrevocable, sufficient deposit of dollars and/or qualifying government obligations. Covenant deposits may not cover accelerated payments, for which the issuer remains liable. German government obligations qualify for specified 2025–2031 Notes, and UK obligations for the 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes. A tax opinion is required; legal defeasance also requires an IRS ruling or change in law. Legal defeasance remains available after covenant defeasance.

nodes.title: Note Settlement, Certificates, and Trustee
nodes.summary: The Notes are generally held in book-entry form through global notes deposited for Euroclear and Clearstream, with no certificates issued for beneficial interests except as described. Under specified conditions—including depositary failure without a successor within 90 days, the issuer’s decision, or a continuing event of default—global notes may be exchanged for definitive certificates in specified euro or sterling denominations and registered as directed by the depositary. The Bank of New York Mellon Trust Company, N.A. serves as trustee; it and its affiliates also maintain banking relationships with the issuer and act as trustee or paying agent for its other and potentially future debt.

summary: Describes the Notes’ series, terms, governing indentures and law; ranking and payment currencies, conversion rules and business days; tax withholding, Additional Amounts and tax-redemption rights; optional make-whole or par redemption; limited covenants and permitted successor transactions; events of default, acceleration, holder remedies and trustee protections; amendment and waiver rules; discharge and defeasance options; and book-entry settlement, circumstances for definitive certificates, and the trustee’s roles and relationships.

title: Subsidiaries of Apple Inc.*
summary: Exhibit 21.1 lists Apple Inc. subsidiaries and their jurisdictions of incorporation, including entities in Hong Kong, the U.S., Canada, China, Ireland, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Australia, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam. It notes that other subsidiaries are omitted because, in aggregate, they were not significant subsidiaries at year-end under Regulation S-K Item 601(b)(21)(ii). The excerpt also begins Exhibit 23.1.

title: Consent of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
summary: Ernst & Young LLP consents to incorporating its October 31, 2025 reports on Apple’s consolidated financial statements and internal control effectiveness into nine specified S-3 and S-8 registration statements. CEO Timothy Cook and CFO Kevan Parekh certify that they reviewed Apple’s fiscal 2025 Form 10-K, that its disclosures are not materially misleading and its financial information is fairly presented, and describe their responsibilities for disclosure and financial controls, evaluations and reporting of changes, deficiencies, weaknesses, and relevant fraud. Both certifications are dated October 31, 2025.

title: CERTIFICATIONS OF CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER AND CHIEF FINANCIAL OFFICER PURSUANT TO 18 U.S.C. SECTION 1350, AS ADOPTED PURSUANT TO SECTION 906 OF THE SARBANES-OXLEY ACT OF 2002
summary: Apple CEO Timothy D. Cook and CFO Kevan Parekh certify under Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 906 that Apple’s fiscal 2025 Form 10-K complies with applicable Securities Exchange Act reporting requirements and fairly presents the company’s financial condition and operating results. Both certifications are dated October 31, 2025. Apple retains the signed original and will provide it to the SEC or its staff upon request.
